proposal: Navarro argues that further negotiation with China is futile and that the next President should decouple economically and financially, adopting a package: extend tariffs to all Chinese products at levels that block them (paced to avoid shortages), incentives to onshore production, closing the de minimis exemption, bars on Chinese state-owned enterprises in federal procurement, bans on Chinese drones and apps, limits on Chinese investment and on U.S. portfolio flows into China, delisting of non-compliant Chinese firms, reduced supply-chain dependence, and fewer visas for Chinese students and researchers. The investment, pension and listing items are tracked separately in c26-06.

status_summary: The administration raised tariffs on Chinese goods sharply in 2025 (a reciprocal rate of 125 percent from 2025-04-09) but then negotiated rather than decoupled: a 2025-11-01 arrangement cut the fentanyl-related tariff by 10 points and suspended port fees and an export-control rule for a year in exchange for rare earth and soybean commitments, and a May 2026 state visit chartered a U.S.-China Board of Trade and a Board of Investment and secured purchase commitments (200 Boeing aircraft, at least $17 billion a year of farm goods in 2026 to 2028). After the Supreme Court ruling, Executive Order 14389 (2026-02-20) ended the IEEPA duties, leaving Section 232 and Section 301 duties in place and the suspension of duty-free de minimis treatment unaffected. A law-firm alert dated 2026-09-24 reports that the Section 122 surcharge expired on 2026-07-24, that most Chinese goods now face a 12.5 percent forced-labor Section 301 tariff, that the Board of Investment remains stalled, and that the Treasury Secretary and China's Vice Premier agreed to extend the trade truce through 2027-01-10, during a state visit by Xi Jinping that began 2026-09-23. On apps, the President delayed enforcement of the 2024 divest-or-ban law through 2025, an order published 2025-09-30 described a qualified divestiture, and a TikTok U.S. joint venture closed on 2026-01-22 with the parent company keeping a stake of nearly 20 percent, rather than the ban the chapter recommends. On visas, the Secretary of State announced a plan in May 2025 to revoke visas of some Chinese students, while the President said the same week that Chinese students would be fine. Procurement bans, supply-chain reduction and the WeChat question were not verified.

timeline.event: Executive Order 14266 raises the reciprocal tariff on Chinese goods to 125 percent and raises duties on low-value shipments from China.

The Secretary of State announces a plan to start revoking visas of Chinese students with Communist Party ties or in critical fields and to tighten screening; the President says Chinese students will be fine and that the administration wants to vet individual students (Bloomberg, via Business Standard, 2025-05-31).

Presidential document published as Saving TikTok While Protecting National Security: it summarizes the executive orders that delayed enforcement of the divest-or-ban law and describes the qualified divestiture process that could lift the law's prohibitions.

White House fact sheet on a trade arrangement with China: the fentanyl-related tariff is cut by 10 points from 2025-11-10, the 10 percent reciprocal rate stays and heightened rates remain suspended to 2026-11-10, shipbuilding port fees and an export-control rule are suspended for a year, and China commits to rare earth licenses and soybean purchases.

TikTok announces that a U.S. joint venture deal valued at $14 billion has closed; Silver Lake, MGX and Oracle each hold 15 percent and the parent company keeps a stake of nearly 20 percent (Politico, republished by Yahoo Finance).
Executive Order 14389 ends the IEEPA duties, including the China synthetic opioid duties and reciprocal tariffs; Section 232 and Section 301 duties and the de minimis suspension are not affected.

White House fact sheet on a state visit to China: a U.S.-China Board of Trade and a Board of Investment chartered; China approves an initial purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft and agrees to buy at least $17 billion a year of U.S. farm products in 2026 to 2028; commitments on rare earths and critical minerals; a Xi visit to Washington planned for fall 2026.

On the second day of Xi Jinping's state visit (2026-09-23 to 25), the Treasury Secretary says the U.S. and China agreed to extend their trade truce through 2027-01-10 from 2026-11-10 (Reuters); a law-firm alert of the same date lists a 12.5 percent forced-labor Section 301 tariff on most Chinese goods, the expired Section 122 surcharge, a stalled Board of Investment and a possible excess-capacity Section 301 action as under consideration.

title: Decouple economically from China with broad tariffs, app and drone bans, and fewer visas
uncertainties: The diverged label rests on the chapter's core claim (negotiation is futile, so decouple) versus a managed-trade posture; several package items were carried out in some form elsewhere (de minimis, drone Covered List additions, outbound investment statute), so a reader could weigh this item as partial rather than diverged. The 12.5 percent forced-labor Section 301 rate on most Chinese goods and the expiry of the Section 122 surcharge on 2026-07-24 come from one law-firm alert; the USTR release of 2026-07-23 does not name China. The truce extension is from Reuters via a syndication site and a secondary summary, and no White House or Treasury document was found. The Politico report gives the parent's stake as nearly 20 percent and the TikTok terms were not read from a primary document. Procurement bans, WeChat, supply-chain measures and any 2026 visa policy were searched for without finding a primary source. Another source on the May 2025 visa announcement (State Department) was not located. Checked systematically on 2026-10-18: Federal Register search of USTR China documents, the Unified Agenda landing page (agency listing not browsable), a congress.gov and GovInfo search by title, the USTR and Treasury newsrooms, and one news search found no action adopting the broad decoupling package; the actions found (managed-trade comment request, Section 301 continuations, truce coverage) are consistent with the diverged staging. S. 1711, the STOP China Act (introduced 2025-05-12 and referred to the Senate Banking Committee with no further action), would bar Transportation Department funds for rolling stock and bus infrastructure from entities tied to China and other named countries; it bears on the procurement item only, is not enacted, and does not change the stage. Passage status of the other bills found was not confirmed.
